title: Digital Forensics
summary: Finding traces after an incident without damaging the evidence.

pages.title: Every action leaves a trace
pages.body:
Digital forensics is the science of collecting, preserving, and analyzing digital evidence so it can be trusted, including in court.

Commonly sought traces:
- System and login logs
- Browser history and recently opened files
- File metadata (when created, modified, by whom)
- Deleted files, which can often still be recovered
- Memory (RAM) contents at the time of the incident
pages.tip: Like a crime scene team: everything is logged and photographed before it's touched.

pages.title: Evidence integrity
pages.body:
Digital evidence changes easily, even just by being opened. So analysts:
- Make an identical copy (disk image) and work on the copy
- Compute hashes (e.g. SHA-256) of the original and copy; if they match, the contents are identical
- Record the chain of custody: who held the evidence, when, and why

Without this, evidence may be ruled invalid because no one can prove it wasn't tampered with.
pages.tip: An evidence hash is the numbered seal on an evidence bag. If the seal differs, someone opened it.

pages.title: Don't erase your own evidence
pages.body:
If you're a victim (hijacked account, scammed, threatened):
- Don't rush to delete chats or accounts
- Take full screenshots with dates, numbers, and URLs
- Keep the original files, not just screenshots, if possible
- Write down the timeline while you remember it
- Report to the platform, your bank, and if needed the police

Organized evidence makes reports far easier to act on.
pages.tip: Cleaning up a crime scene before police arrive is well-meant, but it destroys the clues.

quiz.prompt: Why do forensic analysts work on a copy, not the original?
options: So the original evidence doesn't change
quiz.explanation: Even opening it can change evidence metadata.

quiz.prompt: Hashes are used in forensics to...
options: Prove a copy is identical to the original
quiz.explanation: Same hash = exactly the same content.

quiz.prompt: Chain of custody is...
options: A record of who held evidence, when, and why
quiz.explanation: It proves evidence wasn't tampered with during handling.

quiz.prompt: Your account was hijacked and the attacker threatens you. The right move?
options: Delete all chats for peace of mind
Keep evidence (screenshots, files, timeline) then report
quiz.explanation: Organized evidence helps platforms and authorities act.

quiz.prompt: A normally deleted file...
quiz.explanation: Normal deletion just marks the space as free.

title: Cloud Security
summary: Who's responsible for what, and why so many leaks come from misconfiguration.

pages.title: Shared responsibility
pages.body:
In the cloud (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Google Drive, etc.), security is shared:
- The provider: buildings, physical servers, core network, and base services
- You: data, accounts, who gets access, and service settings

Many people assume "it's in the cloud = it's safe". But if you make a folder public, the provider won't stop you.
pages.tip: Renting an apartment: the building and guards are the manager's job, but locking your unit is yours.

pages.title: The most common mistakes
pages.body:
Most cloud leaks aren't sophisticated hacks, but:
- Storage (buckets, Drive folders) set to "anyone with the link"
- API keys or passwords written in code pushed to public GitHub
- Admin accounts without 2FA
- Excess permissions: everyone is an admin
- Forgotten test servers or databases left open to the internet

Bots constantly scan the internet for mistakes like these.
pages.tip: The safest warehouse is useless if its door is left open with a "come in" sign.

pages.title: Safe cloud habits
pages.body:
For individuals and small teams:
- Regularly review files shared with "anyone with the link" and restrict them to specific people
- 2FA on all cloud accounts, especially admins
- Keep secrets in a secret manager or environment variables, not in code
- Grant minimal access, and revoke it when someone is no longer involved
- Turn on login and suspicious-activity alerts

If an API key leaks: revoke it immediately and create a new one. Deleting the commit isn't enough.
pages.tip: If someone photographed your house key, change the lock. Don't just delete the photo.

quiz.prompt: In the shared responsibility model, data access settings are the responsibility of...
quiz.explanation: The provider guards infrastructure; you guard data and access.

quiz.prompt: The most common cause of cloud leaks is...
quiz.explanation: Misconfiguration is far more common than complex hacking.

quiz.prompt: An API key was pushed to public GitHub. The right step?
options: Revoke the key and create a new one
quiz.explanation: Bots can copy it within minutes; the old key must be disabled.

quiz.prompt: Where should app secrets be stored?
options: In a secret manager / environment variables
quiz.explanation: Secrets in code easily leak through repos.

quiz.prompt: The riskiest Google Drive sharing setting is...
quiz.explanation: Links can be forwarded and opened by anyone.

title: AI, Deepfakes & New Scams
summary: Convincing fake voices and faces, and how not to fall for them.

pages.title: Scams, AI edition
pages.body:
AI makes old scams far more convincing:
- Voice clones from a few seconds of social media video, then a call from your "child" or "boss" asking for a transfer
- Deepfake videos of celebrities promoting bogus investments
- Video calls with fake faces
- Phishing messages with no typos, in polished language

The old sign "the writing is sloppy" can't be relied on anymore.
pages.tip: Scammers used to wear cheap masks. Now the masks look almost exactly like the real face.

pages.title: How to spot them
pages.body:
Deepfakes keep getting smoother, so focus on context, not just looks:
- Urgent requests for money or secrets, especially "don't tell anyone"
- A new number or account, "my old phone broke"
- Video calls cut short, glitches when the face turns or a hand passes over it
- "Guaranteed profit" investment promos from celebrities

Asking the other person to do something spontaneous (turn their head, say the family code word) can help.
pages.tip: Don't just look at the visitor's face. Ask why they showed up at midnight asking for the safe key.

pages.title: Using AI safely
pages.body:
AI is also a useful tool, if used wisely:
- Don't paste secrets (passwords, customer data, internal documents) into public chatbots
- Double-check AI answers on important matters; AI can be confidently wrong
- Be wary of "free AI" extensions or apps that ask for broad access
- Limit public posts of your voice and face if you worry about cloning

And the family code word from LV.00 matters even more in the AI era.
pages.tip: AI is a smart assistant that sometimes makes things up. Give it work, check it, and never hand it the safe key.

quiz.prompt: A voice clone can be made from...
options: A few seconds of audio, e.g. a social media video
quiz.explanation: Today's tech needs only a short sample.

quiz.prompt: A call in your boss's exact voice asks for an urgent, secret transfer. You should...
options: Verify through another channel before acting
quiz.explanation: Voices can be faked; verify through a known number.

quiz.prompt: Why is "sloppy writing" no longer a reliable phishing sign?
quiz.explanation: Focus on context and the request, not language polish.

quiz.prompt: What data shouldn't be pasted into a public AI chatbot?
quiz.explanation: Data you send may be stored outside your control.

quiz.prompt: A celebrity video ad promises "guaranteed 10% daily profit". It's probably...
options: A deepfake and a bogus investment
quiz.explanation: Guaranteed high returns are a classic scam sign.

title: Your Personal Security Plan
summary: Turning every level into a real plan you can start this week.

pages.title: Threat modeling: know yourself
pages.body:
Before adding protection, answer four questions:
- What's most valuable? (bank accounts, photos, work accounts, phone number)
- Who might target it? (random scammers, people close to you, competitors)
- How? (phishing, APKs, a stolen phone, leaked passwords)
- How bad would it be?

Those answers are your threat model. They tell you what to prioritize.
pages.tip: A village home and a city gold shop need different security. Start by knowing which one you are.

pages.title: A 7-day plan
pages.body:
One small step a day:
- Day 1: install a password manager, secure your main email
- Day 2: enable 2FA or passkeys on email, banking, e-wallets, social media
- Day 3: update your phone and laptop, remove unused apps
- Day 4: review app permissions and Accessibility
- Day 5: turn on automatic backups and Find My Device
- Day 6: tidy social media privacy, check your email on haveibeenpwned
- Day 7: agree on a family code word and teach your parents about APK scams
pages.tip: Climbing a mountain starts with one step too. Just keep walking.

pages.title: Be a protector for others
pages.body:
What you learned in Cipher is most useful when shared:
- Help parents and family check their phone settings
- When a scam link lands in a group chat, kindly explain why it's dangerous
- Report scam accounts and numbers to platforms
- Keep learning: threats change, good habits stay

Congratulations, you've reached the edge of the Cipher map. You're not just safer now; you can make the people around you safer too.
pages.tip: One person in the family who understands security is like one person who knows first aid: small, but life-saving.

quiz.prompt: A threat model helps you...
options: Decide what most needs protecting, and from what
quiz.explanation: Security priorities differ for each person.

quiz.prompt: Why secure your main email first?
options: It can reset other accounts' passwords
quiz.explanation: Whoever controls your email can take over many other accounts.

quiz.prompt: What best protects parents from APK scams?
options: Teaching them never to install files from chats, plus a family code word
quiz.explanation: Education and verification habits beat bans.

quiz.prompt: When a scam link appears in the family group, you should...
quiz.explanation: One explanation can protect many people in the group.

quiz.prompt: Cipher's key to long-term security is...
options: Consistent good habits and continuous learning
quiz.explanation: Threats change; good habits keep protecting you.
